children: What happened?
A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks pulled back from the previous session's sharp rally, dragging down technology-heavy indexes.

CNBC reported that the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.5% and the S&P 500 edged lower by 1.2%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline. According to the report, Nvidia shares tumbled more than 7% after soaring 31% in the previous session, while Anthropic tumbled 9%, breaking below its IPO price.

Other artificial intelligence-linked companies also declined, with Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices plunging more than 10%, Broadcom falling 3% and Oracle falling more than 3%, the report said. Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, noted that cloud growth and demand for computing capacity remain supportive, though his team expected greater differentiation between established platforms with strong balance sheets and companies reliant on debt, scarce capacity or speculative growth, according to the report.

When leading artificial intelligence and semiconductor companies pull back sharply, investors often reduce exposure across data center, hardware, and technology infrastructure providers tied to the same spending cycle. Concerns about balance sheet strength and capital intensity can amplify selling in smaller or more leveraged industry peers during a broad tech downturn.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

Zooming in on Xerox

Xerox’s shares are extremely volatile and have had 62 moves greater than 5% over the last year. But moves this big are rare even for Xerox and indicate this news significantly impacted the market’s perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 11 days ago when the stock dropped 8.2% on the news that hot inflation print pushed Treasury yields above 5% and leadership turmoil at Nvidia stoked concerns across its artificial intelligence partner ecosystem. The dual macro and industry pressures mounted after the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the October wholesale producer prices surged 6.5% annually. The data lifted the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield above 5.14%, according to Reuters, fueling expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy and increasing capital costs across corporate IT budgets.

Simultaneously, Nvidia extended a decline from the previous session following the sudden resignation of Chief Executive Jensen Huang, as detailed by Bloomberg. The leadership disruption roiled the chipmaker's ecosystem of server integrators, cloud hosting providers, and technical consultancies, raising worries that hardware delivery timetables and enterprise AI integration contracts will stall. When hardware delivery schedules become uncertain and financing costs jump, enterprise clients defer signing deployment contracts, compressing the near-term revenue visibility of the services firms contracted to roll out AI infrastructure.

Xerox is down 67.3% since the beginning of the year, and at $0.81 per share, it is trading 77.8% below its 52-week high of $3.62 from September 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Xerox’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at only $39.85.
